I am glad that the Prime Minister has taken this, perhaps the first, opportunity of introducing this matter to the house. So far as the second part of the resolution is concerned, I am rather doubtful of this proposal. It is proposed that private bills after going to a standing committee shall be placed on the order paper for third reading. It would appear from this resolution that on these private Ibills the house will not go into committee of the whole, and consequently the members of the house as a whole will not have the opportunity of securing the information that perhaps will be secured in the standing committees. To that we take objection.
I would like to call the attention of the house to an anomaly that this proposal is going to create if it is carried through. We are all here representing various constituencies, and in the final analysis every member of this house is on an equality, but when it comes to the question of bills introduced by private members for private persons or corporations, such bills have precedence over bills of a public nature that are introduced by private members, and under those circumstances, no matter how desirous any member of this house may be of trying to secure the passage of needed legislation of a public nature, he is to all intents and purposes blocked by the rules of the house. If there is going to be an opening up, to facilitate the passage of private legislation through this house by ensuring that it shall be voted upon,
I submit to the Prime Minister and to the house that the private member introducing public legislation should be put on a parity with the private member introducing private legislation. We have no objection to this matter going to a committee for consideration, but if that committee in its report makes a further discrimination as between public and private legislation, we in this corner of the house are going to take very strong objection to it.	.

subtopic: PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF PRIVATE SECRETARIES

speechtext:
Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No 7, to amend the Civil Service Act (private secretaries).
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Private secretaries, appointment.

subtopic: PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF PRIVATE SECRETARIES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF PRIVATE SECRETARIES
speechtext:
The object of the amendment is to give to private secretaries who are not already in the civil service the privilege of entering therein, but only in the event of the ministers, whose secretaries they are, ceasing to act in that capacity. The amendment is also to apply to the secretary of the leader of the opposition. If my hon. friends will consult the notes which accompany the bill they will see that the question of private secretaries has been on many occasions a matter of concern to the house, inasmuch as there are many different clauses or sections of the act dealing with it. The difficulty is to reconcile the very natural desire of a minister to have a confidential secretary with the equal desirability of assuring a certain degree of permanency in the service to the gentleman who fills that position. Before 1906 the private secretary to a minister was a member of the civil service and received additional consideration of $600 a year. I may point out, however, that prior to that time the minister could appoint anyone to the civil service, and therefore, when
152	COMMONS
Civil Service-Private Secretaries
he desired to have the services of a secretary, he could first have him appointed to the service. At that time the remuneration was $1,500, to which could be added the $600 which was the special allowance for a private secretary; or, in the alternative, the minister might choose a man from the service and pay him the additional gratuity. The revised statutes of 1906 embodying the Civil Service Act contain the provision, section 81, that any member of the civil service might be appointed private secretary to the head of a department and might be paid an additional salary, not exceeding $600 a year, whilst so acting. That confirmed the provision which existed before, but owing to the fact that the Civil Service Commission had taken over appointments to the civil service the minister was deprived of the right to appoint his own secretary. In 1908 a change was made in the act, the amendment, as will be seen in the explanatory notes, reading:
39. Any person chosen by a minister to be his private secretary may, without examination and irrespective of age, be appointed for a period not exceeding one year, and paid as a clerk in subdivision B of the second division, and after one year's services as such secretary he shall be deemed to be appointed to such rank.
That gave to the minister the privilege of appointing one man of Ms own choice; after one year of service this man would become a member of the civil service in a certain subdivision, and would receive a salary ranging from $1,200 to $1,600 plus the additional $600 which I have mentioned, and which always has been a special grant to secretaries belonging to the service. In 1912 the section was amended with regard to the subdivisions of the service open to such secretaries; this gave them a larger salary and a better position. In 1918 that section was replaced by the section now in the act, which reads as follows:
Any person may be appointed by a minister of the crown or other member of the government to be his private secretary, and if sueh person does not hold a permanent position in the civil service he may be paid such salary as the governor in council may prescribe, if he holds a permanent position in the public service he may be paid an additional salary not exceeding six hundred dollars a year whilst so acting.
The position to-day is that a minister may appoint his secretary at a salary prescribed by order' in council or else take a man already in the service and add to the salary of that man the $600. The objection which has been made to that situation is that a young man becoming private secretary to a minister has no assurance of permanency in the service; at any moment he may lose his posi-
tion. The objection which was made to the former provision allowing a minister to ch-oose his own secretary who, after one year, became a member of the service, was this: If a minister wanted to abuse the statute, or if he only made full use of it, he could choose a new secretary every year and allow the former secretary to enter the service, and I am quite sure that this provision was amended for the purpose of preventing any such action. If members of the committee will look at the present bill they will see that we have sought to remedy that possible objection by adding a provision that in the case of a minister ceasing to be a minister, and in that case only, the private secretary of such minister will be appointed to a permanent position in the public service, and I do feel that 'this is a very reasonable proposal to make. It is not intended at all to give the ministers any opportunity of appointing men to the service without passing the necessary examination, to any greater extent than is required to meet this particular situation. In fact no privilege at all is afforded the minister, because only when they cease to be such do their private secretaries receive an appointment in the service. If hon. members will look at the sections I have read, which are printed in the bill, they will find that while this may seem a small question to some of us it has received the consideration of the house on many occasions in attempts to find a solution for it. The proposal we now bring forward is .that if a minister chooses-as his private secretary a man from outside the service, such secretary will have the security of an appointment to the permanent service if, for one reason or another, his minister ceases to act as such.
It may be pointed out that this will add many civil servants to the different departments, but I do not think that point arises; if a minister picks a man from his department, instead of appointing a man from outside the service, that man will have to be replaced in any event. For instance, if instead of choosing my secretary from outside the service I went to the companies branch, the naturalization branch or some other branch, of my department for a man, that man would be replaced by someone else, and when I ceased to act as a minister the man I selected from my department as secretary would have a right to return to the service. So I do not think this proposal will add to the number of public servants; it will merely provide as a qualification for permanent appointment in the service the number of months or years given by a private secretary to the work of his department. I appeal to the reason of

Civil Service-Private Secretaries
the committee and ask if an examination in geography, history and other subjects is a better qualification for employment in the service than the work put in by a private secretary who handles all the correspondence of the minister, who is in touch with the heads of all branches and who is thus put in a most excellent position to become familiar with all matters pertaining to that department.
I am in the bands of the committee if any further information is desired, but I wish to add merely as an act of courtesy that while the secretary to the leader of the opposition is included in this bill, that was done without the least suggestion from either the leader of the opposition or his secretary; it was done by the government in the view that the gentleman occupying that position is in exactly the same class as the private secretary to a minister. In that connection I might point out that in most cases when the leader of the opposition becomes the Prime Minister, which is the ambition of every leader of the opposition, his private secretary goes with hi;m, -while the private secretary of the Prime Minister usually becomes the private secretary of the leader of the opposition. So.I do not think there is any probability of a great many public servants being appointed in this way.
We feel great sympathy for the young men who work with us and who give us, the government and the country their very best services, yet we know that by a vote of this house, or an event which might affect only one minister, one or more of them may be deprived of their positions in a day. I do think that the work of a private secretary is a better qualification for appointment to a position in the service than any examination wdiich might be conducted by the Civil Service Commission, and I commend this small bill to the sincere attention of the house.

Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence) moved that the house go into com-rpittee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Militia Pension Act in respect to the computation of the amount of pension payable to officers retired compulsorily or seconded, to be based upon the average annual amount of pay and allowances during the three years immediately preceding retirement, and to amend the procedure for computing the pension for an officer who has served as a member or associate member of the defence council for a period of not less than three continuous years.
Explain.

The object of the bill
which will be founded upon this resolution is as set out in the resolution. The first part 
introduces a principle which will change the existing order so far as the pensions of officers are concerned. As hon. gentlemen know, the provisions of the Superannuation Act are that civil service pensions shall be based on the average of the salary for the last three years of service. This same principle applies to the pension payable to non-commissioned officers and men, but for some time the pension payable to officers has been based on the amount they receive at the time of their retirement. This permits a situation whereby pressure may be brought to bear to increase the salary just before an officer retires, in order that the pension might be increased. It is sought to bring the pension payable to officers under the same principles as apply to civil servants, noncommissioned officers and men.
I do not think the second part of the resolution is a very important matter. The members of the defence council are generally staff officers or senior officers who are appointed under the regulations for four years. These positions are generally regarded as the highest which can be attained in the service. At the end of the four-year period, or whatever extension there is, they have to go back to some position which pays a lower salary, with the result that the amount of their prospective pension is cut down. The proposal is to allow those officers who have attained sufficient seniority and efficiency in the service to take positions as members or associate members of the defence council, to have their pensions, when they retire, based on the average of the three years' salary received by them as members of the defence council.

Do the
officers who benefit by the pensions contribute in proportion to the rank or the salary that they receive?
They contribute a percentage of their salary.

Might this not work an
injustice in some cases having regard to those who, say, yesterday may have been pensioned on the basis of six years' salary and those who the day after to-morrow may be pensioned on the basis of three years' salary? Perhaps the committee is the proper place in which to ask that question.

I may say that the provision is that this is not to apply to officers now in the service.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

Military Pension Act
One effect of this resolution will be to prevent the giving of a promotion at the end of a period of service for the purpose of giving increased pension.

That is quite right. Such a promotion would only increase the average amount. That is to say, the extra amount received on account of such promotion would be totalled in the three years' pay and the whole divided by three and promotion therefore would not have the same effect as it has at present.

The minister will
have to answer some questions from the service. If officers are allowed to come here and put in, say two, three or four years, how is the minister going to explain the refusal of an increased pension to certain ones who put in three or four years' service during the war? There are both non-commissioned officers and officers who, after they had retired on pension, came back and gave three or four years' service during the war. For that they have received nothing in the way of an increased pension. The minister will have to meet criticism in this regard if he is going to give an increased pension to some person who goes to headquarters and serves three or four years there.

I am afraid I have not
made myself clear. I am talking only about those who are members of the defence council. The other method would be to allow those members to remain and to retire as members of the defence council. In many cases that may be advisable as regards the individual, but it is hardly fair to other officers in the service who are qualified and who ought to have their turn at headquarters. Therefore it is felt, even though the members of the defence council are qualified, that in the interests of the service it is perhaps well to have what one might call demotion, at least reduction in salary to go back to a district. Yet it is felt that in view of seniority and qualifications, they might well be paid a pension based on the salary they have received as members of the defence council.

I am pointing out
that the minister will receive criticism in regard to those people to whom a pension has been refused.

A distinction is made between officers of the same rank in the service. That is to say, an officer serving in command of a district with a rank perhaps senior to that of a member of the defence council, might draw a smaller pension than an officer of a junior rank.

That is the case to-day.
Members of the defence council are not paid on the basis of rank; they are paid on the basis of salary.

It seems to me that the
object as outlined in the first part of the resolution may be defeated if the second part carries. As I understand the matter from the explanation given by the minister, the average annual salary is to be taken into consideration in computing the pension. The minister quite properly said that one of his reasons for bringing down this legislation was that he wished to prevent pressure from being brought to bear upon the department and the minister to have rather rapid promotion given at the end of an officer's military career; but as I understand the matter, members of the defence council and associate members, whatever they may be, obtain slightly higher salaries than officers carrying on their ordinary duties. Therefore in another way pressure will be brought to bear upon the minister to make officers members of the defence council, say for a month or two or three months so that they may benefit on retirement by receiving an increased pension. I may be wrong in that assumption, but I am simply pointing out to the minister and to the committee that this might be one of the consequences of passing the second portion of the resolution.

I endeavoured to foresee
that very situation, and when the bill is introduced my hon. friend will see the provision-and it is also in the resolution-that a man mu9t be a member of the defence council for three years before this applies. He cannot qualify for an increased pension by being a member of the defence council for three, six or nine months.

Take the case of a district
officer commanding who has held the appointment for, say one year. Will this amendment make any difference in the pension which he will draw?

It would in the case of
a district officer commanding who enlists after this measure is passed. My hon. friend will understand that I am one of those who believe as far as possible in preserving what ma3' not be contractual rights but at the same time what may be the understanding when a man enlists. There are times, however, when the public interest requires some change. I understood that this was a somewhat far reaching change and therefore provision is made that this legislation shall not apply to any persons now in the service; it shall apply only to those who enlist afterwards.
Military Pension Act

That is just the point. If we are going to amend1 the Pension Act, it would be a good thing to amend it so that an officer would draw a pension based upon the average salary over a period of three years, because if we do that, it will prevent the very thing which I mentioned at the outset, namely, giving an appointment to a man after, say long service, in order that he may retire on a higher rate of pension. If the minister will make a search he will not have very far to seek to find that that has been done.

I agree with that thoroughly, and I am endeavouring to correct it for the future. I would feel some hesitation about doing away with the principle under which these officers have been serving and are in the service at the present time. I would be glad indeed to concur in my hon. friend's suggestion except that it seems to me it perhaps interferes with at least some possible moral claim that an officer at present in the service might have to have the terms of service maintained during his period of service.

I am afraid I do not follow the minister. I should like him to point out what is in the contractual relation which would justify a man in expecting a promotion just before retirement in order to draw a higher rate of pension.

There is nothing to justify that except what my hon. friend has just suggested, namely, that there are instances where promotion has been made immediately prior to retirement. There are instances where promotion has been made just before retirement.
Why not extend the amendment to make that impossible?

Because it would be altering the situation with regard to officers now in the service. I want to assure my hon. friend .that that will be discouraged by administration, but after this provision becomes effective there will be no purpose for pressure being brought to bear.

Will it be stated
in the bill that this provision will refer only to officers enlisting from now on?

Yes.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Ralston thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 33, to amend the Militia Pension Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Hon. PETER HEENAN (Minister of Labour) moved:
subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: That the Technical Education Act be amended to provide that any balance of the ten million dollars appropriated under this act unexpended on the 31st March, 1929, shall remain available during any one or more of the five succeeding fiscal years, but no portion thereof shall be paid to any province after the 31st March, 1934.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: I would suggest to the ministry that when these resolutions are moved, an opportunity should be given to us for discussion.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
I did not think it was
necessary to deal with this matter in detail, as full information can be given when we get into committee on the bill. As hon. gentlemen will recall, the Technical Education Act was passed in the year 1919. It provided for assistance to the provinces in the matter of technical education for a period of ten years. Some of the provinces did not take advantage of the act when it was first passed, and the purpose of the amendment now is to extend the act for a further period of five years to enable the provinces which did not take advantage of the act to earn their proportion of the grant.
In the year 1910 a royal commission was appointed to inquire into industrial training and technical education. That commission reported in the year 1913, and recommended that assistance be given to the provinces to the amount of $30,000,000, the grants to be used for technical education, agricultural instruction and industrial research. The Agricultural Instruction Act expired some years ago and on its expiration it was extended for one year. The Technical Education Act expires in March of this year. The government is now going into industrial research quite extensively, involving an expenditure far greater than the amount that was originally recommended for technical education. During the Dominion-Provincial conference it was made quite clear by the representatives of the provinces that they did not desire the federal grants to *be continued or extended if there were any tags on them. Rather they felt that any federal assistance that was given should be by way of general subsidy.
As I have said, I can go into details more fully when the bill is before the house. Briefly, the purpose of the amendment is to

Technical Education Act
extend the period for five years, in order to enable those provinces which did not take advantage of the act in the first place to earn their portion of the grant.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
At the opening of the
session I placed on the order paper a question asking the ministry if they had received requests for the renewal of the $10,000,000 appropriation made in 1919, and asking further if the government had given any consideration to the matteT. The Prime Minister replied that the government had received such requests, and in answer to my Last question about giving consideration to the matter, his reply was:
Yes. Notice has been given of legislation to be brought down during the present session providing for the amendement of the Technical Education Act. This legislation will set out the intention of the government.
I had hoped from the nature of that reply that the legislation might have been of the character alluded to in the first question, namely, an extension or renewal of the grants for technical education. Little need ibe said in support of the contention that these two grants-I think there have been two grants of 810.000,000 each-for technical education have proved of immense value to the Dominion of Canada. If that is the case, I believe the immediate future would warrant in even a stronger manner the continuance of the grants, because never in the history of this country was there such a broadening of opportunity for young Canadians who have been technically trained as the future seems to hold forth. We have developed in recent years huge water-powers, with the result that industrial expansion is assuming very considerable proportions, which we hope will go on increasing from year to year, and offering at least some opportunity to stay the exodus of our brighter young men to the wider opportunities offered in the United States. Therefore, to my mind, if we were warranted in 1909 in granting $10,000,000 for assistance in the matter of technical education, and again in 1919, we are doubly warranted at this time in continuing the grants. It has just been suggested to me that I am in error in saying there were two grants, and that only one grant of $10,000,000 has been made. I had thought that there were two, but I am subject to correction. But in any case my point is that at this time we are warranted more than ever before in making this further grant.
I have before me the report of the legislative program of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, dated January 8, 1929.
While it may be that we cannot at all times agree with all of the suggestions of the Trades and Labour Congress, I believe that their utterance in regard to technical education will be received with favour and approval by almost every member of the house. It reads as follows:	.
Reenactment Technical Education Act 1919. It is to be regretted that the government has not yet seen fit to reenact the Technical Education Act of 1919 which expires on March 31 this year, as we are convinced that without federal assistance technical educational activities in the various provinces will be restricted. We believe that the Premier of Ontario stated the case clearly, when in a press statement published May iast, he said:
Then they quote:
The Technical Education Act passed by the Dominion in 1919, did not encroach on the prerogative of the provinces. It did not assume to take control of any schools; it left the responsibility for the administration of technical schools strictly to the provinces to which it belongs by constitutional right.
The act was, in fact, a financial measure dealing with federal funds. It undertook to use federal money to promote and assist technical education in Canada. In other words, the Dominion sought to induce the provinces and the municipalities, on the assurance of federal assistance, to undertake a very expensive service to the country, on a larger scale than would otherwise be possible.
That is the end of the quotation of the statement by the Premier of Ontario. Then the Trades and Labour Congress proceed with their statement:
Reiterating our statement presented Iast year we would emphasize that technical education is an essential part of apprentice braining, and as such, lays the foundation for industrial efficiency, which reflects itself in Dominion revenues. For this and similar reasons we again advance the opinion that the Dominion government could properly continue grants for technical education and urge the enactment of legislation to make this possible when the act of 1919 expires.
I particularly direct the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister, whose sympathy I know is in line with this sort of legislation, and of the Minister of Labour to this point made by the Trades and Labour Congress: that technical education is an essential part of apprentice training.
In other words, the Trades and Labour Congress draw attention to the advisability of promoting in Canada what is the common practice in the older countries of Europe, development of apprentice training among the various industrial activities of this Dominion. I think we have been woefully neglectful in this regard. Certainly in some industries which are highly organized and well established apprentice training has been carried
Technical. Education Act

on, but in many branches of artisan activity apprentice training has not been practised. For instance, this winter I noted in Vancouver- whether it is followed elsewhere or not I do not know-that among the building trades they have introduced a system of apprentice training. It has been in operation for the last few years, and I was advised only a few weeks ago that the results have been eminently satisfactory, that many young men taken from the technical school established under this vote of 1919 have been introduced into the building trades and are proving to be most efficient and capable workers, and in fact are likely to become the natural successors of the contractors and builders. That is a splended work. That alone is an excellent result to achieve. But that is only one narrow branch of activity. The technical education provided for in the provinces extends 'to many branches of activity, and so I think, Mr. Speaker, we should very seriously consider extending the grant before disposing of the question.
There is another phase to which I wish briefly to refer. It is the statement by the Premier of Ontario which I have already quoted:
The Dominion sought to induce the provinces and the municipalities, on the assurance of federal assistance, to undertake a very expensive service to the country on a larger scale than would otherwise be possible.
Now, that is not a complaint, it is merely a statement of fact, that after an extensive study by the Dominion parliament, through a commission, extending over a period of four years, a very elaborate report was made. It was a report of nation-wide importance. The report was recognized by the government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and by the succeeding government of Sir Robert Borden, as of sufficient importance to warrant this Dominion as a whole taking it into consideration. The report is in the library and is a very elaborate and a very excellent piece of work. Then parliament made this grant of ten million dollars. With what result? Unfortunately I have not under my hand the details, but suffice to say that most if not all of the provinces took advantage of the grant and established technical schools. I refer again to Vancouver merely because I am more familiar with it than with any other city. Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. King), the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) and I think the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) were in Van-IMr. Stevens.]
couvev and saw the magnificent school which has been established there. It is a huge series of buildings built by the province and the city with the assistance of this grant. In those buildings is now housed the school which has been organized over the last three years. The school at first was established in a comparatively small building in the centre of the city. Now it is housed in this magnificent building, and scores of young boys of high school age are attending and receiving technical education. It was a big capital investment. This is not a poor man's plea, but I put this to parliament. Parliament having undertaken the investigation of this subject, parliament having secured a report thereon, and parliament having acted on that report, surely now parliament is justified in considering whether or not the results to date justify a continuance of the grant. That I think is a fair question, I submit to the government that practically all of the provinces have played the game in the matter; they have established these institutions and have made excellent progress. Now I suggest to the government that they should for another ten-year period continue the grants in order to ensure the further establishment of this valuable service for the young men of the Dominion.
One other thought, and I now direct my appeal more to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The minister, since his appointment to that important office, has given very excellent and intelligent attention to the question of industrial research, which is a subject we have often discussed in parliament and which has been very close to my own heart. He has done very creditable work; he has made efforts much greater than he has been permitted to see carried to fruition. This has been due to lack of funds. Nevertheless he has done, as I say, very good work, having made a splendid start in the last few years. He is going ahead with industrial research-what for? And, by the way, may I express the hope that parliament will double his grant this year. The estimates are not yet down, but I hope that such provision will be made. Now, for what purposes is the minister carrying on this reasearch? He is doing it to assist in the process of converting our vast raw resources in Canada into something like a valuable product for sale to the world at large. Briefly, that is his object. It is to discover new methods of utilizing these materials; to assist industry in expanding its business and organizing itself on a better basis; to find new uses for our raw materials, and so forth. His object is to im-

Technical Education Act
prove methods, to extend and to broaden the uses of our raw materials, to enlarge our markets, and to increase the efficiency of our plants. That, roughly speaking, is what he is doing. Now, why do we not correlate all this with the improved efficiency of the youth of the country to enable them to take advantage of the opportunities to be created by the minister in the splendid efforts he is making in the industrial research branch?
I say to the government that no money voted by this parliament could be more wisely spent than in an honest, intelligent extension of industrial research, followed, and supported or supplemented, by a grant to technical education to enable our young people to take advantage of the opportunities which we trust will be presented through the expansion of our industrial activities.
I will not speak any longer. I think that this subject is one which has absolutely no partisan aspect; it is something which is vital to the life of the normal Canadian citizen. There is no group of citizens in this country more entitled to consideration than those who will be affected by this legislation. And who are these people? Not the rich; not those who can afford an extended university training; they are the boys and girls belonging to the families of honest, intelligent citizens throughout the country, whose means are restricted and with whom the necessity of earning a livelihood is imminent at all times. It is the boys and girls of such families who will be affected by this legislation. And they are the very backbone of the nation. This question applies not only to the wage earners of the nation, in the broad general sense of the term; it applies to intelligent, enterprising and, shall I say, ambitious artisans, workers and tradesmen. If there is any social work under the sun which is more important than this I should like to know what it is. There is nothing more important than the social work of helping a man or a boy to help himself. I sincerely hope, therefore, that the government will not allow this session to proceed further without giving to the house an assurance that this question of extending the grant to technical education will be taken up in earnest and not merely given " consideration " -because that is a political term sometimes used to hide the desire to evade; all of us have used it. I hope we shall get an assurance that the matter will be given sympathetic study, based upon a desire to meet the needs and requirements of this new branch of education.

I am very glad to be able to endorse what the last speaker (Mr. Stevens) has said. I speak
feelingly on this subject because I think it was pretty well recognized a few years ago that the system of apprenticeship in industry was almost a thing of the past. Within the last two or three or five years, however, there has been a change; and probably to-day we have more apprentices working under the old apprentice system in connection with various branches of industry in the country than we have had for some considerable time. The reason for this, to some extent-at all events, in the maritime provinces-is the fact that we have had technical night schools which have given our mechanics an opportunity to obtain some technical education during their apprenticeship period which was not previously available. Only the other day I was speaking to the superintendent of one of our largest works who made this remark: "The one thing that I am more thankful for than anything else is the fact that my father had the good sense to insist upon my serving an apprenticeship as a machinist." Knowledge thus gained is invaluable ; it does not cost anything except the effort to obtain it. We have to-day in the maritime provinces, in the town from which I come and in others as well, night technical schools; and in some of our works there is an arrangement whereby apprentices can put in two or three hours a day getting technical instruction at no cost to themselves; in other words, the establishment in which they are employed' pays their wages while they are so engaged. That is a matter of very considerable importance, and I would stress what has been so eloquently expressed by the hon. member who has spoken, as to the extreme importance of technical education in this country. I know of no movement more entitled to the support of the minister than that under consideration, and I trust that such steps will be taken as will result in the continuation of and a large increase in the appropriation for technical education in connection with such workmen as I have referred to.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
May I for a moment associate myself with those who have already spoken, first, in commending the government and the minister upon bringing forward the resolution which is before us, and1 in suggesting that it might go further and be adopted as a permanent policy. As civilization advances and as we more and more, in our industry, adopt mechanical contrivances of an intricate character, the need for special training to be given to the men and women who are to operate such machinery and carry on the industries making use of it becomes increasingly important. I might
Technical Education Act

suggest, also, that there is perhaps no work which is more truly Canadian in its scope. It is true that part of the responsibility for such training rests with the provinces; but it is my opinion, and long has been, that it is more incumbent, in the very nature of things, upon the federal government than upon the provinces themselves; for the lines which separate one province from another are purely imaginary, and the boys and girls trained in one province may possibly-nay probably-find employment in other parts of the country. That is the reason, or one of the reasons, why we urge that this policy of assisting in technical education be extended and made permanent, and that it shall not take merely the form of temporary grants.
No money has been better spent and no action of the government has been more highly appreciated than in respect to this very work. As has been said, this is work which is not only non-partisan in character but is very widespread in its application. I have had the pleasure of meeting in different ranks of life and in different forms of industry some of the young men who have gone through the technical schools and have had the opportunity of obtaining technical instruction. I believe that if this opportunity were afforded more of our young people it would go some distance at least in solving the problem of unemployment, because after all unemployment is mainly found among those people who have had no training for any special work and who show no aptitude for the more intricate forms of labour.
Then there is another matter. More and more we are finding that there is not only keen competition within the boundaries of our own country, under which the efficient win out while the inefficient are trampled down, but there is competition between the different countries themselves and in the long run, in my opinion that country which will wisely train the young men and women who will do the work of the morrow and fit them for the battle of life will succeed in this international competition in which we are always engaged.
I have no intention of taking up more of the time of the house, but I would like very much to see this principle extended and this resolution offered in such a form, either now or in the near future, that we might look forward to a continual and an increasing opportunity being given to our young people all over Canada to fit themselves for a proper place in the industrial life of what we hope will be one of the strongest and finest industrial countries as well as the finest agricultural country in the world.
[Mr. Speakman.J

I wish to contribute just a few sentences to discussion of this subject which I think interests all thoughful members of the house, and that means all members. On a number of occasions, both last year and this year, this question has been brought to my attention by the board of education of my city, which is one of the large labour centres among the smaller cities of western 'Ontario. The board of education is very anxious to see the Technical Education Act continued as it has been up to the present. Last year when the matter was up I put a number of questions to the Prime Minister and drew the conclusion from his answers that the government had decided positively not to renew that act. I believe that was the attitude of the government last year, but without any desire to do other than good to the people who profit by this, if the government carry this resolution to-day later in the session I would like to see them bring in a further resolution with the intention of carrying on this assistance as it has been carried on in the past.
One of the reasons why, before the war, the German nation was so successful in gaining supremacy in so many lines of endeavour was that it went deeply into research work; they trained their workmen and their trade commissioners and others to meet their needs. Largely beoause of that and, in my opinion, because of their fiscal system, they were rapidly becoming the leading industrial country of the world, and were foremost in a number of lines of endeavour. So I wish to put myself strongly on record as ready to support the government in any effort they may make to carry on this technical education assistance as it has been carried on in the past.

I rise to support the very able presentation of the case by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I do not know of any question before parliament to-day which is of more concern to the rank and file of the people of British Columbia than the possibility of losing this aid to technical education Most of us have received resolutions from different public bodies such as the Local Council of Women, parents' and teachers' associations, the Young Mens' Christian Association, Lions clubs, school boards and other organizations asking that this aid be continued, and I observed that the legislative program of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada strongly emphasized the need for the continuation of this aid to technical education.
I am not sure that I caught exactly what the Minister of Labour meant when he pre-

Technical Education Act'
sented his ease this afternoon, but I understood him to say that at the conference of premiers some sort of tentative understanding was reached whereby the different provinces would forego their request for this aid in return for some adjustment of the provincial subsidies. I would like to ask the minister if that is a correct understanding of what he said.

by the representatives of the provinces that they did not want any further grants which required federal supervision; they desired that any assistance should be given by way of a general subsidy.

Then I want to urge upon the government the fact that this grant is of such far-reaching importance to the youth of this country that the government could not take a wiser step than to ear-mark that grant for technical education, for which it has been given during the last ten years. It is not going to do technical education any good to make some arrangement or understanding with the premiers of the provinces that you are going to increase their subsidies and allow them to do what they wish with the money instead of ear-marking it for technical education, and I think if any such idea exists it should not be allowed to continue.
I want to emphasize to the Prime Minister and the government the good effect of this grant as far as the provinces are concerned; I want to urge the need for it at present, and I believe that unless some sort of parental control is exercised by this government this grant may never find its way to the support of technical education. Public interest in this matter is extensive, its importance to the country is clear, but the resolution in its present form would indicate that a certain balance of this money is to be available during the next five years. Would the minister tell us how much that balance is and what portion of it will be received by British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
It is not often that I
have the privilege of agreeing with practically every word spoken from the other side of the house, but in this instance I think I can say that I am in entire accord with practically every expression of opinion given in the house this afternoon with regard to the importance of industrial and technical education and the great service rendered to this country by the institutions which have been established for that purpose. The government is not in disagreement with hon. gentlemen opposite as to the importance of industrial training and technical education. Our only difference is that we believe the time has come when the provinces themselves should carry on the obligation which they undertook at the time the grants of the federal government were originally made to them. While technical education is to be fostered and maintained and developed, it should from now on, we believe, be fostered and maintained and developed by the provinces themselves. The government has been liberal in the assistance given the provinces from the federal treasury to aid in the introduction o>f these schools and in obtaining the necessaiy personnel for teaching purposes, and in that particular the obligation the Dominion undertook at the outset has been completely fulfilled.
I believe I have followed the development of industrial training and technical education in Canada as carefully as any hon. member of this house. As minister of labour some years ago, it was my privilege to ask this house to appoint a royal commission to study industrial training and technical education and to gather data on the subject which could be placed at the disposal of the provinces. I remember there was a great deal of opposition at that time even to that simple request. The opposition was based on the ground that the federal parliament had nothing to do with the subject of education, that under the British North America Act education was a matter which belonged exclusively to the provinces. In reply to that contention the government of the day stated that they did not propose to have the federal government become responsible for education, technical or otherwise, but that what they desired to do was to gather through one agency the data which would be helpful to the provinces

Technical Education Act

in the subsequent development of an industrial training and technical educational system. It was felt that the federal government, through the Department of Labour, might appoint a commission which would visit not only the different provinces of Canada and ascertain the needs for technical education but visit Europe also and report upon the systems of technical education in operation there, and that the information thus gathered might then be placed at the disposal of all the provinces. It was clearly on that understanding that the commission on industrial training was appointed. There was no thought at the outset that the federal government would be called upon to go further than simply to supply the information to the provinces which would enable them to develop their educational systems along lines of industrial training and technical education.
In the report presented by this commission, attention was drawn to the fact that at that time there were no duly qualified teachers for schools of industrial training and technical education, that it would take some little time to train a corps of teachers. It was also stated that there were no buildings in which the work of technical education could be carried on, that the provinces would be put to the expense of building technical schools, equipping them, and training teachers to carry on that all-important work. An appeal was made to the federal government to assist the provinces by a grant for a limited number of years, a grant which would enable a personnel of teachers to be brought into being during the time the provinces were establishing the schools and securing the necessary equipment.
That was the basis on which the Dominion undertook to give assistance to the provinces for a series of years, and it was never contemplated that that assistance was to run on indefinitely. If it had been, this would have been made very clear at the time. I would point out that if such were the intention this parliament might as well say at once that it is going to take over education. Is it the duty of the federal parliament to enter the field of education, whether education be elementary, primary or secondary, or scientific, or is it the duty of the provinces? I do not think there is any doubt about its being perfectly clear, under our constitution, that it was intended the provinces should undertake the work of education.
Education does not mean simply teaching on the old lines of the public and high schools; it means teaching in accordance with the ever-developing range of knowledge and

the needs of communities and their interests. The work of education to-day has an emphasis on the industrial and technical side such as it has never had heretofore, and the provinces should be meeting that particular need. I believe they are meeting it very successfully, but up to the present they have been meeting it in part with the assistance of this parliament.
I wish to draw the attention of this house particularly to one fact. When it was recommended in the report of the technical education commission that grants be made, there were not the obligations on the federal treasury which have been imposed upon it since. The report was made prior to the war and since that time there has been an increase in the public debt of Canada of over $2,000,000,000. The annual interest payment amounts to $125,000,000, which is equal to what it took to carry on the whole business of the government of Canada at the time Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into office. This obligation has come during the intervening years, and it is not an obligation that is shared in any way by the provinces of Canada; it falls exclusively and entirely upon this federal government. Had that obligation been apparent at the time the commission made its report, I doubt very much if there would have been a recommendation to this parliament further to assist the provinces in the work of technical education. But in addition to that, there are other obligations which we have assumed and which the provinces have not assumed at all. We have assumed the obligation of pensions payable, first of all, to men who have returned from overseas disabled, and to the dependent relatives of those who fell. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establiShment was brought into being to carry out the work of re-establishment. This department has now been changed to a department of pensions and health. There is an annual war pension bill amounting to many millions of dollars, which is an obligation this parliament did not have at the time it undertook to assist the provinces in the matter of technical education. The provinces have not assumed any part of that obligation; they have not assumed an additional dollar's burden as a result of the war.
We have not only undertaken the payment of war p^isions in an ever-increasing amount, but we have undertaken to assist the provinces in another field, a field related to industry-namely old age pensions. We are making to the provinces for old age pensions large grants from the federal treasury, which grants will be increasing from year to

year. They were not even contemplated at the time the bill was passed giving to the provinces for a period of ten years, grants for industrial training and technical education.

If it helps them financially it will be placing the Dominion in a relatively less favourable position with respect to its finances. We are considering the transfer to the western provinces of their natural resources. We are considering the transfer to British. Columbia of lands in the railway belt and Peace River block. In the United States I understand there is an agreement between the federal government and the various state governments whereby they both donate certain sums of money for technical education. This agreement is known as the Smith-Hughes bill, which was passed in the federal house in 1917. I see no reason why we cannot have a similar agreement. I was very much interested in the remark made by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) that the great prestige of Germany has been due to the interest taken in technical education by the German government. I heartily concur in that remark. I have in my hand a statement with regard to technical education in Germany. At the present moment I do not know who the author is, but I think hon. members present will be interested in it. It reads:
This progressive country also provides splendid technical colleges for the training of engineers, commercial universities for the preparation of men who shall direct the business and industry of the empire, navigation schools, mining schools, industrial art schools, leather schools, textile schools, etc. There is some sort of education offered for every kind of human activity and every grade of worker. The older traditional education is not slighted and generous provision is made for classical education in public schools and universities. [Mr. Luckkovich.J
There is an absolute faith among all the people in the power for good education and everywhere honour is accorded to any kind of trained man commensurate with this degree of learning. Is it any wonder that Germany has forged to the forefront of civilized nations in the last thirty or forty years? In 1876 the manufactures, the inventions and the foreign commerce of the separate states were far below those of England and France. To-day, United Germany stands in the forefront rank of the nations of the world in industrial production and she clearly leads all the nations in the application of science to the industry and to the arts. Her position is all the more remarkable because this result has been achieved in a country in which [DOT]he agricultural and mineral resources are not
eat and in the face of the burdens, due to long and costly wars, to maintenance of a great army and to the draining of a large part of its population through emigration. The Germans themselves are proud to proclaim that the greatest single instrument in accomplishing their wonderful industrial growth has been technical education.
A few years ago, a number of prominent German manufacturers, educationists and public men, made an extensive tour in the United States with the idea of finding out how serious a competition the latter nation might prove in the future struggle for world trade. Their consensus of opinion was that the United States possessed greater natural resources, a superior factory system, workmen of greater energy, industry and mechanical skill and cheaper railway transportation. Notwithstanding all these advantages, the German experts thought even the existing grip of America on international trade would tend to weaken. They commented on the absence of any adequate system of special education for commerce, banking or foreign trade in the United States. The meagreness of technical education, the trifling annual contingent of chemists, engineers, trained foremen, educated dyers, weavers, electricians and mechanics, as compared with the throng of lawyers, physicians, dentists and unspecialized graduates of colleges seemed shortsighted and improvident. The foreign investigators concluded that on the whole the "American danger" had been greatly exaggerated and that a steadfast adherence by Germany to the technical educational policy and commercial method now in practice will leave the fatherland little to fear in future competition with American manufactured goods.

Mr. Speaker, although a
number of members have spoken in favour of this resolution, I should not like to let this opportunity go by without urging that not only should this grant be extended, but that the policy of granting assistance by the Dominion government to technical education should be adopted. The labour organizations across the country are most heartily in favour of action of this kind. In fact I can hardly understand the attitude of the government in bringing to a sudden close an experiment which has proved so eminently successful. Those engaged in industry and agriculture as well as educationalists and the general public are in favour of technical education. It seems to me that if the men in control of big industry have at all considered the modern industrial situation they ought to be holding up both hands in favour of this kind of thing.
I am afraid that the British North America Act may be the death of us. It is invoked almost daily in this house as an excuse for inactivity by the federal government. It is

quite true that, technically, the provinces have jurisdiction over education, but I submit that an altogether different situation exists to-day from that which existed in this country sixty years ago. At that time education consisted very largely in teaching the three R's to the children in the little local scboohiouses. No one will say that that situation any longer exists. We have passed from being a merely agricultural community to a community in which technical training becomes absolutely necessary to success. Not only in those lines which are generally distinguished as industrial, but in agriculture itself the highest form of technical training is essential. We must recognize that the resources of the provinces have not increased as rapidly as the new responsibilities. In the earlier days the program of education did not involve any considerable outlay.
Some years ago I had the opportunity of serving on a commission on technical education appointed by the government of my own province. In that connection I could not but be impressed by two or three things that in fact have remained with me through the years. One was that our boys and girls had very little opportunity of qualifying for any of the more highly skilled and more remunerative positions in Canada. Nearly all our skilled craftsmen are imported, chiefly from England and Scotland, some from the continent of Europe. We Canadians are settling down to be hewers of wood and drawers of water, or we are going into business and professional life; certainly we are not contributing any very large number of people to the skilled trades. I do not think that is a satisfactory condition of affairs. I should like to see our workers in the very forefront of modern industry.
We should remember that the old apprentice system is a thing of the past, and so our boys have no chance, except in very occasional industries, of serving apprenticeship in the old way. As a result thousands are graduated from our schools to go into what have been termed blind alley occupations.
Our investigations brought another thing home to me-that Canada was lagging far behind in the educational developments which are taking place in Europe and in most of the American states. After touring some of the states and seeing the splendid technical institutions established there, I must confess that when we returned to Canada-I think for the first time in my life I felt ashamed of my own country; we were so many years behind the stage of advancement in many other places. Why should

Technical Education Act
Canada be behind in these things? I take it that we are in the forefront along certain lines. We boast of our progress, but why cannot our progress be uniform? Why cannot we excel in some of these matters which are so eminently important? It may seem to some that we are spending an undue time in the house discussing this question, but we spent parts of three days discussing whether or not we should have titles in Canada. There seems to be an indifference, however, when we come to discuss matters that are of vital importance to the future of 'the country.
I take it no one suggests that it is impossible for the Dominion government to assist the provinces in carrying on their educational activities. It is quite open to the Dominion to make grants along the line that has been followed in the past. Such grants have been welcomed by the provinces. The question is rather one of allocation of responsibility. The policy to be decided is, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) indicated: Should the Dominion government pay for work of this character? He suggests that the Dominion is already overloaded. I believe, however, that a careful study of the situation will show that a great many of the services in the country are being carried on to-day by the provinces. It is quite true that the federal administration carries a very heavy debt incurred through the war; but I do not think that the Prime Minister is correct when he says that the provinces have not shouldered one extra dollar of the burden due to the war. Anyone familiar with the upkeep of the hospitals, for example, will recognize that there are enormous burdens laid upon the provinces by the war.
Let us take other matters that are initiated by the Dominion government; take for instance the question of immigration. We bring in tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of immigrants. It is true that the Dominion government spend a good deal in order to get the immigrants here; but the amount they spend getting the immigrants here is nothing to the amount the provinces have to spend in educating them and their children after their arrival. Members resident in the east can hardly realize the extent of the burden that must be carried by the western provinces in educating the children of newly arrived immigrants, the burden entailed in the special types of education which must be provided for them. All that burden is thrown upon the provinces. Or again, we have a Department of Health here; but the greater part of the burden of taking care of the health of immigrants devolves upon the
provinces. I do not see any reason why it should be so. It may be true, again though this is not altogether certain that technically, under the British North America Act, the matter of health may have been left to the local communities; but the framers of our constitution did not contemplate the introduction of hundreds of thousands of new citizens into the country, and their being left to be cared for Ideally. The same is true with regard to charity and the care of the unemployed, and all that sort of thing. Technically, charity may fall within the purview of the provinces; but the vast extent to which some of our provinces have helped the unemployed in these present days is an altogether different matter from what was contemplated by those who originally drew up the provisions of the British North America Act. Our provinces are carrying a tremendously heavy load. How do they meet this responsibility? The Dominion has larger revenues at its disposal; and, more than that, the Dominion has it in its power, through indirect taxation, to levy taxes in a way which is not possible for the provinces. And it is through this indirect taxation that we derive the greater part of our revenues to-day. I would suggest, therefore, that since the Dominion government is such a large producer of revenue it is quite right that the provinces should1 be able to secure a very considerable proportion of that revenue for purposes of this kind, which are not merely local but essentially national in character.
I do not propose to inquire as to what was the original purpose when this grant was made ten years ago. I do not think we ought to go back and ask what was in the mmds of those who were willing at that time to assist technical education. I take it that during the past ten years we all ought to have learned a great deal more about the importance to the country of technical education, and whatever might have been thought originally, ten years ago, to-day it is incumbent upon this parliament to take the larger view of such matters as this. I hope the government will reconsider its whole policy in this regard, recognizing that side by side with the grants to research work there should be large grants for the training of the men who, we hope, will be able to carry on industry successfully with the information which may come to us from the research bureau.

In Nova Scotia over half of the total revenue of the province goes towards the upkeep of highways. Who ever dreamed at the time of confederation that public health would require the colossal expenditures that are necessary to maintain that branch of the public service up to the proper modern standard called for to-day? The same applies not only to technical education but to all other forms of education. It seems that the elastic sources of revenue were placed at the disposal of the federal government-sources such as the sales tax, the income tax, customs, excise tax and many others-while the inelastic sources were left to the local governments. The federal government has the opportunity to extend the sources of its revenue, but the local governments are not in that happy position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that scientific knowledge is not of service to the masses of the people?

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: He did not say any such thing, but he did say that technical education assists the masses of the people and that industrial research belongs to the aristocrats of learning; those who have had university education and who are capable of carrying on industrial research work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Does my hon. friend call Doctor Banting an aristocrat?

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
He is a medical man and the graduate of a university. I referred to aristocrats of learning, men who had university degrees, while the men who will be benefited by this grant are the young men coming from the schools, as they come in Calgary and other places I have seen in various parts of this country, where they are learning just what they used to learn in the old days as apprentices in machine shops and such places. There they become familiar with the operation of machinery; they learn about lathes; they take up other kinds of technical work which belong to the work of the ordinary young man who goes out as a machinist, a mechanic, a carpenter or what not, to make his living in that branch of human activity.
Industrial research is just as much a matter of education as technical education; industrial research means men trained in universities and schools of learning. And what are we doing in Canada with respect to industrial research? In the province of Ontario you will find millions of dollars being provided by private individuals and by the taxpayers for this work, and as far as that province is concerned we are simply duplicating that effort. No attempt is made to correlate the activities in industrial research with respect to the provincial departments of education and their universities. The Prime Minister said he was wholly in accord and deeply in sympathy with the observations made with respect to technical education, but I venture to say that if this house, with the whips removed, were to vote on the question whether
or not this grant should be continued, if we voted as ordinary Canadians representing Canadian constituencies, there would not be ten
votes cast in opposition to the continuance of this grant.
We are told that we cannot afford it. I will save it; I will save one-quarter of it in the amount spent on automobiles used by ministers in this city last year. Look at the public accounts; we spend about $2,000,000 a year in the education of Indians. Do you mean to tell me that when we can find that money we cannot find $1,100,000 for the technical education of the young men and young women of this country? Do you mean to tell me that with revenues exceeding $400,000,000 you cannot find $1,100,000 for the technical education of the young people of Canada? That is absurd.
Then you tell me you have increased the grants to the provinces. Of course you have. Last year we took $152,000,000 from the people of Canada, in customs revenues alone, and the contribution that we have made in the way of financial compensations and adjustments to the provinces by reason of that fact is not out of proportion to tire increased revenues which have been occasioned by the customs tariffs since confederation. Everyone knows that. I say this is not a question of economy; it is the worst kind of economy to cut down this grant, because you are lessening the power of the young men and women of this country to produce new wealth; moreover you are increasing the incentive for them to leave the country to obtain the technical education which is denied them here. Further, it is apparent to every thoughtful man that the provinces cannot carry this burden.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
For the simple reason
that they are carrying such a burden with respect to highways, the development of agricultural resources, the increased cost of government, the maintenance of their universities and so on that unless they have some support of this kind they cannot carry on this work.

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Surely my hon friend does not want to tell the house that all the provinces are in such a condition that they cannot look after this work?

subtopic: PAYMENT TO PROVINCES OP UNEXPENDED BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
I wonder if the hon.
gentleman has looked at the act? The provinces are required to provide proper buildings; they have done so and in many cases borrowed the necessary money. A limited part of that grant is made available for the purposes of the buildings, but having done this
Technical Education Act

for a period of ten years they are suddenly confronted with the shutting off of that grant,
which amounted to $10,000 for each before the question of population arose at all. The smallest province received $10,000 just as the largest province received $10,000; up to that amount there was equality as far as the grant was concerned, and then the balance was adjusted according to the population as shown by the last census. That enabled every province to make some provision with respect to this work. In the maritime provinces, certainly, from information I received during the period I was there last year, I gathered that if they had to carry the burden placed upon them with respect to old age pensions, which, mark you, was not of their own seeking in the first instance but was placed upon them by this federal government before they could get any grant from the federal treasury, the amount in one case will reach several million dollars. The demands for money for highway services are so great that they are unable to maintain that service adequately unless they receive increased grants. The increased subsidies that have been granted, even if they were ample to enable them to maintain the ordinary services, are not sufficient to enable them to carry on this particular service without depriving other services of necessary revenue.
I think my hon. friend from Saskatoon will realize how difficult it has been to balance the budgets of the provinces, even the richest and most powerful. Recourse has been had to the profits derived from the sale of strong drink in order to balance the budget in many instances. In fact I find that matter is plainly stated in many of the provinces I have visited during the last twelve months. Is it impossible for us, as members of parliament, to find ways and means to provide $1,100,000 for technical education?
I would suggest to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Finance that instead of arriving at the definite conclusion that this will not be provided, they take the will of parliament regardless of party, for it is not a party question. Let the will of the majority of this parliament determine whether or not we shall continue to pay that grant. If that is done I am satisfied this house will make provision for the payment for another ten years of this $1,100,000 for technical education. This work has accomplished much, and if we are able to provide the money I am sure it will be of incalculable benefit.
I could go into this matter at much greater length, but I do not think it is necessary to

do so. My only suggestion is that instead of closing the door we permit the will of this house to determine the question regardless of any other consideration but the public interest in the development of technically trained men to take their place as future citizens of this country.
Motion agreed to, on division, and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
